title: Syphilis in Obstetrics and Gynaecology
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Treponema pallidum, crucial in obstetrics due to its severe impact on pregnancy outcomes. Early diagnosis and treatment are vital to prevent congenital syphilis and maternal complications. It presents in stages, with diverse clinical manifestations.

sections.p: Syphilis is a chronic systemic infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. In obstetrics and gynaecology, its significance lies in its potential for vertical transmission, leading to congenital syphilis, and its impact on maternal health. Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical suspicion and serological tests.
b: Primary syphilis: painless chancre at inoculation site.
Secondary syphilis: systemic symptoms, rash, condyloma lata, granulomatous hepatitis.
Latent syphilis: asymptomatic, diagnosed by serology, divided into early (<1 year) and late (>1 year).
Tertiary syphilis: gummas, cardiovascular syphilis, neurosyphilis.

sections.p: Syphilis progresses through distinct stages, each with varying clinical presentations and implications for pregnancy. Staging is critical for determining appropriate treatment regimens and assessing the risk of transmission.
b: Early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent): highly infectious, high risk of vertical transmission.
Late syphilis (late latent, tertiary): less infectious, but still poses risk of vertical transmission and severe maternal complications.
Neurosyphilis can occur at any stage and requires specific treatment.

sections.p: The sole cause of syphilis is infection with the bacterium Treponema pallidum. Transmission primarily occurs through sexual contact with an infected individual, but vertical transmission from mother to child during pregnancy or childbirth is also a major concern.
b: Unprotected sexual contact with an infected partner.
Vertical transmission from an infected pregnant mother to her fetus (congenital syphilis).
Rarely, through contact with infectious lesions or contaminated blood products.

sections.p: Clinical presentation varies significantly with the stage of infection. In pregnant women, symptoms may be subtle or absent, highlighting the importance of routine screening.
b: Primary: painless ulcer (chancre) at the site of inoculation, often on external genitalia, cervix, or anus, appearing 10-90 days post-exposure.
Secondary: diffuse maculopapular rash (often on palms and soles), condyloma lata (wart-like lesions in moist areas), lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise, headache, sore throat, granulomatous hepatitis.
Latent: asymptomatic, diagnosed solely by positive serology.
Tertiary: gummas (granulomatous lesions affecting skin, bone, or organs), cardiovascular syphilis (aortitis, aortic aneurysm), neurosyphilis (meningitis, stroke, tabes dorsalis, general paresis).

sections.p: Diagnosis relies on serological tests. In low-resource settings, rapid plasma reagin (RPR) or venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) tests are often the initial screening tools, followed by confirmatory treponemal tests.

t.b: Screens for active infection and monitors treatment response. A positive result indicates active or recently treated syphilis. Titres correlate with disease activity.
Confirms syphilis infection. A positive result indicates past or present infection. These tests usually remain positive for life, even after successful treatment.
Screens for co-infection with HIV. Syphilis and HIV often co-exist, and HIV can alter the clinical course and serological response to syphilis.

t.a: Lumbar puncture (CSF VDRL, cell count, protein)
t.b: Diagnoses neurosyphilis. Indicated in patients with neurological symptoms, treatment failure, or HIV co-infection with late-stage syphilis.

sections.p: Untreated syphilis, especially during pregnancy, carries severe risks for both mother and fetus. Early recognition of these red flags is crucial for timely intervention.
b: Stillbirth or neonatal death due to congenital syphilis.
Hydrops fetalis, prematurity, or low birth weight.
Congenital syphilis manifestations: hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, rash, rhinitis, bone abnormalities, neurological damage.
Maternal complications: neurosyphilis, cardiovascular syphilis, gummatous lesions.

sections.p: Treatment of syphilis, particularly in pregnancy, is primarily with penicillin, which is highly effective and prevents congenital syphilis. The specific regimen depends on the stage of syphilis.
b: Primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis: single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G. Penicillin is chosen for its efficacy and ability to cross the placenta.
Late latent or tertiary syphilis: three weekly intramuscular doses of benzathine penicillin G. A longer course is needed for established infection.
Neurosyphilis: intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G for 10-14 days. This regimen achieves adequate penicillin levels in the cerebrospinal fluid.
Penicillin allergy: desensitization to penicillin is recommended for pregnant women, as it is the only proven effective treatment for preventing congenital syphilis.
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction: a self-limiting febrile reaction that can occur after the first dose of penicillin, due to spirochete lysis. Reassure the patient and manage symptomatically.

sections.p: Regular follow-up is essential to ensure treatment success and monitor for re-infection. Prevention strategies focus on screening, partner notification, and safe sexual practices.
b: Repeat VDRL/RPR titres at 3, 6, and 12 months post-treatment (and every 3 months during pregnancy) to confirm a four-fold decrease in titre, indicating successful treatment.
Screening of all pregnant women at the first antenatal visit and again in the third trimester (or at delivery) in high-prevalence areas.
Partner notification and treatment of all sexual partners from the preceding 90 days (for early syphilis) or longer (for late syphilis).
Promotion of safe sexual practices, including condom use and reducing the number of sexual partners.
HIV testing should be offered to all individuals diagnosed with syphilis.

sections.p: The diverse presentations of syphilis can mimic other conditions, making accurate diagnosis challenging. Clinical acumen and appropriate serological testing are key.
b: Genital herpes: painful vesicles and ulcers, often recurrent, unlike the painless chancre of primary syphilis.
Chancroid: painful, ragged ulcers with tender lymphadenopathy, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi.
Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV): transient, often unnoticed ulcer followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy.
Pityriasis rosea or drug eruptions: can mimic the rash of secondary syphilis, but lack other systemic features.
Scabies: pruritic rash, but without the specific features of secondary syphilis.

sections.p: Interpreting syphilis serology requires careful consideration, as false positives and negatives can occur, particularly in certain clinical contexts or stages of infection.
b: False-positive non-treponemal tests (VDRL/RPR): can occur in autoimmune diseases (e.g., SLE), malaria, HIV, pregnancy, or other infections. Requires confirmation with treponemal tests.
False-negative non-treponemal tests: can occur in early primary syphilis (before antibody development) or in late-stage syphilis (prozone phenomenon).
Treponemal tests (TPHA/FTA-ABS) remain positive for life, even after successful treatment, so they cannot be used to monitor treatment response.
HIV co-infection can alter serological response, sometimes leading to atypical titres or delayed seroreversion.

faq.a: Yes, syphilis is curable with appropriate antibiotic treatment, typically penicillin. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial for a complete cure and to prevent complications.

Untreated syphilis in pregnancy can lead to severe complications including miscarriage, stillbirth, prematurity, low birth weight, and congenital syphilis in the baby, which can cause lifelong health problems.

faq.q: Is it possible to have syphilis and not know it?
faq.a: Yes, syphilis can be asymptomatic, especially in the latent stage. Symptoms can also be mild or mistaken for other conditions, making routine screening important, particularly in pregnant women.

exam: A 24-year-old pregnant woman, G1P0 at 12 weeks gestation, presents for her first antenatal visit. Routine screening reveals a positive RPR titre of 1:32 and a positive TPHA. She reports no symptoms. What is your immediate management plan? — Confirm diagnosis with a treponemal test if not already done. Stage the syphilis (likely early latent). Treat with a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G. Counsel on partner notification and treatment. Schedule follow-up RP

You are reviewing a neonate born to a mother with untreated late latent syphilis. The baby appears healthy at birth. What investigations would you perform, and what is your management approach? — Investigate for congenital syphilis: RPR titre (quantitative), complete blood count, liver function tests, long bone X-rays, CSF analysis (if indicated). A patient with a known penicillin allergy is diagnosed with primary syphilis during pregnancy. How would you manage her treatment? — Penicillin desensitization is the preferred approach for pregnant women with penicillin allergy and syphilis, as penicillin is the only drug proven to prevent congenital syphilis. Consult with an allergist for desensitization protocol, then administer benzathine penicillin G.

Describe the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in the context of syphilis treatment and how you would manage it in a pregnant patient. — It's an acute febrile reaction (fever, headache, myalgia, rash exacerbation) occurring within 24 hours of syphilis treatment, due to rapid spirochete lysis. Reassure the patient, it's self-limiting. Manage symptomatically with antipyretics and analgesics. In pregnancy, monitor for uterine contractions, but it rarely causes preterm labor.

What are the key differences in serological testing for syphilis that guide diagnosis versus monitoring treatment efficacy? — Non-treponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) are used for screening and monitoring treatment response, as their titres decrease with successful treatment. Treponemal tests (TPHA, FTA-ABS) are used for confirmation of infection and usually remain positive for life, so they are not useful for monitoring treatment efficacy.

A pregnant woman presents with a painless genital ulcer. What are your differential diagnoses, and how would you differentiate them from primary syphilis? — Differentials include primary syphilis, chancroid, genital herpes, and lymphogranuloma venereum. Primary syphilis presents with a painless, indurated ulcer (chancre) and often non-tender lymphadenopathy. Genital herpes causes painful vesicles that ulcerate. sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused obstetric‑gynaecology history and systematic exam can identify syphilis manifestations, rule out mimics, and assess complications such as neurosyphilis or congenital infection.
b: Timing of sexual exposure, number of partners, condom use, and any recent genital lesions.
Prior syphilis testing or treatment, including dates and regimens.
Pregnancy status, gestational age, and any obstetric complications (e.g., stillbirth, pre‑eclampsia).
HIV status, TB exposure, and other STIs; ask about antiretroviral therapy if HIV‑positive.
Drug allergies, especially penicillin; ask about previous desensitisation attempts.
Systemic symptoms: fever, malaise, weight loss, rash, joint pain, neurologic signs (headache, visual changes).
Obstetric history: prior miscarriages, neonatal deaths, or congenital syphilis in previous pregnancies.

t.a: Inspection for chancre or condyloma lata
t.b: Detects primary or secondary lesions; a painless, indurated ulcer suggests primary syphilis, while moist, flat‑topped papules in intertriginous areas suggest secondary disease. Cannot differentiate stage without serology.

t.a: Palpation of lymph nodes (inguinal, cervical, axillary)
t.b: Tender, rubbery nodes support secondary syphilis; non‑tender nodes may be seen in primary stage. Does not confirm infection.

t.a: Neurologic exam (cranial nerves, gait, sensation, reflexes)
t.b: Identifies signs of neurosyphilis (e.g., Argyll Robertson pupil, tabes dorsalis). Absence of findings does not exclude early neurosyphilis.
Granulomatous hepatitis in secondary syphilis may cause palpable liver or spleen; not specific to syphilis.
Detects fetal growth restriction secondary to placental infection; cannot determine cause without further testing.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Serology remains the cornerstone; each test answers a specific diagnostic or monitoring question. When a test is unavailable, use the next best alternative and interpret with clinical context.
b: Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) – screening and quantitative monitoring; titre ≥1:8 in pregnancy warrants treatment, four‑fold fall by 6 months indicates adequate response.
Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TP‑PA) – confirmatory treponemal test; reactive result remains positive for life, does not indicate activity.
VDRL on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) – diagnostic for neurosyphilis; reactive CSF VDRL OR CSF WBC >5 cells/µL + protein >45 mg/dL confirms neurosyphilis.
Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA‑ABS) – confirmatory; useful when TP‑PA unavailable.
Dark‑field microscopy of ulcer exudate – direct detection of spirochetes; positive only in primary lesions, not feasible in most low‑resource labs.
PCR for T. pallidum (if available) – detects organism in ulcer or CSF; high specificity, limited sensitivity in blood.
Complete blood count and liver function tests – assess for anemia, hepatitis, or drug toxicity; abnormal results do not diagnose syphilis.

t.b: Quantifies disease activity; a four‑fold decline (e.g., 1:32 to 1:8) by 6 months signals successful therapy. Persistent high titre suggests treatment failure or reinfection.
Confirms exposure; remains positive lifelong, so cannot be used to monitor response.
Positive result confirms neurosyphilis; if negative but CSF WBC >5 cells/µL + protein >45 mg/dL, neurosyphilis is still diagnosed.

t.a: CSF WBC >5 cells/µL and protein >45 mg/dL
t.b: Abnormal CSF parameters support neurosyphilis when VDRL is non‑reactive; must be interpreted with clinical signs.
Direct visualization of spirochetes confirms primary syphilis; negative result does not exclude disease if lesion is old or sample inadequate.
Detects bacterial DNA; a positive result confirms infection, useful when serology is equivocal.
Use VDRL as an alternative quantitative non‑treponemal test; interpret titres similarly.

sections.p: Staging integrates clinical features, timing of exposure, and serology. Severity guides treatment duration and need for CSF evaluation.
b: Primary syphilis – painless chancre ≤3 weeks after exposure; positive non‑treponemal test, treponemal test reactive.
Secondary syphilis – systemic rash (palms/soles), condyloma lata, mucous patches; occurs 4–10 weeks after infection; high RPR titres.
Early latent – seropositive ≤1 year after infection, no symptoms; still highly infectious, especially in pregnancy.
Late latent – seropositive >1 year, asymptomatic; lower infectivity but still transplacental risk.
Tertiary syphilis – gummas, cardiovascular disease, or neurosyphilis occurring >3 years; requires prolonged therapy.
Neurosyphilis – any stage with CSF VDRL reactive or CSF WBC >5 cells/µL + protein >45 mg/dL; may present with meningitis, tabes dorsalis, or ocular involvement.
Severity classification – based on stage and presence of organ involvement (e.g., neurosyphilis = severe).

sections.p: Several genital or systemic diseases mimic syphilis lesions or serologic patterns; careful history, exam, and targeted tests separate them.

t.b: Painful vesicles/ulcers; Tzanck smear or HSV PCR positive, serology for syphilis negative.
Painless beefy‑red ulcer without lymphadenopathy; tissue smear shows safety‑pin organisms, syphilis serology negative.
Small painless ulcer followed by tender inguinal buboes; NAAT positive for Chlamydia, syphilis serology negative.

t.a: Secondary skin eruptions (viral exanthema, drug rash)
t.b: Rash may involve palms/soles but lacks condyloma lata; negative syphilis serology or low RPR titre.
Palmar/sole rash can occur; ANA positive, anti‑dsDNA, complement low; syphilis serology negative.

t.a: Pregnancy‑related pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP)
t.b: Pruritic papules, no systemic symptoms; syphilis serology negative, skin biopsy non‑specific.

sections.p: A structured approach ensures prompt treatment, prevents fetal infection and reduces complications.
b: Confirm diagnosis with a reactive nontreponemal test and a treponemal confirmatory test.
If pregnant or early syphilis, give benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose; desensitise if allergic.
For late latent, tertiary or neurosyphilis, give aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18‑24 MU IV daily for 10‑14 days.
Monitor serologic response: four‑fold RPR titer drop by 6 months (early) or 12 months (late).
Repeat CSF examination at 6 months if neurosyphilis was treated; repeat only if symptoms persist.
Escalate to specialist referral for treatment failure, persistent CSF abnormalities, or pregnancy complications.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Recognising adverse reactions and interactions prevents harm and maintains efficacy.
b: Jarisch‑Herxheimer reaction: fever, chills, headache within 24 h of penicillin; treat with antipyretics, reassure, continue therapy.
Penicillin allergy: risk of anaphylaxis; perform skin testing, desensitise if needed, avoid macrolides as they do not prevent congenital disease.
Ceftriaxone: possible biliary sludge in neonates; monitor liver function if prolonged use.
Tetracyclines (if used for alternative): contraindicated in pregnancy and children <8 y; avoid due to teeth staining.
Alcohol: no direct interaction with penicillin but may worsen Jarisch‑Herxheimer symptoms; advise moderation.

sections.p: Early identification of severe disease guides timely referral and additional therapy.
b: Neurosyphilis: CSF VDRL reactive or CSF WBC >5 cells/µL with protein >45 mg/dL; refer for IV penicillin and repeat CSF at 6 months.
Congenital syphilis with signs (hydrops, hepatosplenomegaly, rash): start IV aqueous penicillin 50 000 U/kg q12 h for 10 days; involve neonatology.
Cardiovascular syphilis (aortitis, aneurysm): refer to cardiology; penicillin alone does not reverse structural damage.
Gummatous disease causing organ dysfunction: treat with IV penicillin; consider surgical consultation for destructive lesions.
Treatment failure (persistent RPR ≥4‑fold rise after 6 months): reassess compliance, HIV status, and consider retreatment.

sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions modify presentation, test performance and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV co‑infection: higher RPR titres, slower serologic decline; repeat CSF if neurological symptoms or treatment failure.
TB co‑infection: overlapping constitutional symptoms; ensure separate TB treatment; avoid drug interactions with rifampicin.
Malnutrition: may blunt skin rash; monitor for anemia and support nutrition during treatment.
Pregnancy: placental transfer of penicillin is safe; avoid all other antibiotics for definitive therapy; monitor fetal growth.
Diabetes: peripheral neuropathy may mask neurosyphilis signs; maintain glycaemic control during infection.
Renal failure: penicillin dosing unchanged for IM benzathine; adjust IV aqueous penicillin if severe accumulation risk.
Liver disease: penicillin is hepatically safe; avoid hepatotoxic alternatives.
Herbal remedies (e.g., neem, garlic): may interfere with immune response; counsel patients to discontinue during therapy.

sections.p: Tailored strategies address the needs of vulnerable populations and resource‑limited settings.
b: Children with congenital syphilis: give aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50 000 U/kg IV q12 h for 10 days; if unable to IV, use benzathine penicillin 50 000 U/kg IM weekly for 3 weeks.
Pregnant women: single dose benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM for early disease; three weekly doses for late latent; desensitise if allergic.
Elderly: monitor for Jarisch‑Herxheimer reaction and cardiac comorbidities; ensure renal function before IV therapy.
People with HIV: use same regimens but expect slower serologic response; repeat CSF if neurological signs persist.

facts: Primary syphilis: painless chancre, 3–6 weeks incubation
Secondary syphilis: maculopapular rash on palms/soles, condyloma lata
Early latent (<1 year) and late latent (>1 year) are asymptomatic
Neurosyphilis: CSF VDRL reactive OR CSF WBC>5 cells/µL with protein>45 mg/dL
Congenital syphilis: treat newborn with aqueous penicillin G 50,000 units/kg every 12h for 10 days
Early syphilis in pregnancy: single IM benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU
Late latent/tertiary: aqueous crystalline penicillin G 10–14 days
Penicillin allergy: desensitise then give benzathine penicillin
RPR titer decline 4-fold after treatment indicates cure
RPR non-reactive + TP-PA reactive in treated patient suggests past infection

vivas.q: What is the hallmark of a primary syphilis chancre?
vivas.a: A painless, indurated ulcer with a clean base, often on genitalia, cervix or anus.

vivas.q: Which rash is pathognomonic for secondary syphilis?
vivas.a: Diffuse maculopapular rash involving palms and soles, often with condyloma lata in moist areas.
CSF VDRL reactive OR CSF WBC>5 cells/µL with protein>45 mg/dL; both criteria must be met.

vivas.q: What is the first-line treatment for early syphilis in pregnancy?
vivas.a: Single IM dose of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU; desensitise if penicillin‑allergic.

vivas.q: Why is a single dose of benzathine penicillin preferred over weekly dosing?
vivas.a: It achieves adequate serum levels, is simpler, reduces compliance issues and is evidence‑based.

vivas.q: Interpret an RPR titer of 1:32 after treatment.
vivas.a: A 4‑fold decline from baseline (e.g., 1:128 to 1:32) indicates adequate response; no decline suggests treatment failure.

vivas.q: What is the management of a penicillin-allergic patient with primary syphilis?
vivas.a: Desensitise to penicillin, then give benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM once; monitor for Jarisch‑Herxheimer reaction.

vivas.q: How would you differentiate a syphilitic chancre from a herpes ulcer?
vivas.a: Chancre is painless, indurated, clean‑sanded base; herpes is painful, grouped vesicles that rupture.

vivas.q: Why is the RPR non‑reactive but TP‑PA reactive in a treated patient?
vivas.a: TP‑PA remains positive long after cure; RPR reflects current activity; this pattern indicates past treated infection.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a positive RPR in a pregnant woman at 12 weeks?
vivas.a: High risk of vertical transmission; requires immediate treatment with benzathine penicillin and fetal monitoring.

vivas.q: Explain the Jarisch‑Herxheimer reaction and its management.
vivas.a: Sudden fever, chills, myalgia 1–2 h post‑treatment; give paracetamol, monitor vitals; reassure patient.

vivas.q: When should CSF be repeated in an HIV‑positive patient with neurosyphilis?
vivas.a: If treatment failure or persistent neurological symptoms; not routinely at CD4<350.

vivas.q: What are the key bedside history questions for a suspected syphilitic ulcer?
vivas.a: Onset, pain, location, sexual history, prior STIs, pregnancy status, exposure to untreated partners.

vivas.q: What is the recommended follow‑up schedule for a treated syphilis patient?
vivas.a: RPR at 6, 12, 24 months; decline of at least 4‑fold indicates cure.

vivas.q: Why is a single dose of benzathine penicillin adequate for early syphilis?
vivas.a: It provides sustained therapeutic levels for 3 weeks, covering the infectious period.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of secondary syphilis?
o: Maculopapular rash on palms and soles
mcqs.e: Painless chancre is primary, not secondary.

mcqs.q: A pregnant woman at 20 weeks has a non‑reactive RPR but a reactive TP‑PA. What does this indicate?
mcqs.e: TP‑PA remains positive after cure; RPR non‑reactive indicates no active infection.

cases.v: A 32‑year‑old primigravida presents at 14 weeks with a painless ulcer on the vulva. She reports a recent unprotected sex with a partner who has a history of STIs. RPR is reactive 1:128. TP‑PA is reactive.

qs.a: Single IM dose of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU.
Repeat RPR at 6, 12, 24 months; monitor fetal growth and ultrasound.

mistakes: Assuming penicillin‑allergic patients can be treated with doxycycline for early syphilis
Misinterpreting a reactive RPR as cure without a 4‑fold decline
Failing to desensitise before penicillin in allergic patients
Ignoring the need for CSF VDRL in suspected neurosyphilis
Assuming a non‑reactive RPR rules out past infection
